speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have
seen a report which has given me some concern; I do not know whether it has come to the government's attention or not. It relates to the Chicago drainage canal diversion and to the interpretation given the recent judgment of the Supreme Court of the United States by the Chicago authorities and, so far as I know, by others generally. It is well known that a limitation was placed on the diversion by the Supreme Court judgment, which limitation was believed here to be a real limitation of the very serious diversion from our waters which had up to then taken place, and the still more serious diversion in immediate prospect, it being a limitation to 8,500 cubic second feet. The interpretation which I have seen as intended to be acted upon is this: that the 8,500 cubic second feet, disastrously serious in itself, is to be applied to the drainage exit alone, that is to say, it is not to include the waters diverted by the alteration of the course of the Chicago river, which course has been changed from a flow into the lake-the natural flow-to a flow at a nearer point into the Chicago canal. It also involves an exclusion of the water taken for purposes of water supply. That is to say, the interpretation is said to be 8,500 cubic second feet for drainage alone, exclusive of 1.300 cubic second feet represented by the turning of the course of the Chicago river, and 1.200 cubic second feet more taken for the purposes of water supply. This total would be 11,000 cubic second feet, or worse than we ever understood as having been the actual practice. I would like to ask the government if they have had any information to this effect, and if so, what steps the government have in mind to bring to a head, or at least to some prospect of solution, this very dreaded and calamitous state of affairs.

I understand
that under the arrangement made last week we are to discuss under this item the question of the export of power, and if I am correct in that I wish to make a few remarks in that connection. Since we last discussed this matter a return has been tabled by the government dealing with the question of the export of Carillon power. It is a long return, covering a good many years. Since the return was tabled the gentlemen of the press, in the first place, considered it, and immediately after that the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Ethier) was fortunate enough to be ab'e to get his hand upon, it, and he conveyed it after that to the Minister of Trade and Commerce-
Who had it for fifteen minutes.

-who tells us he had it for fifteen minutes. I do not know where it was in the meantime, but I do know that the people who asked for it and wanted it were able to get it at something like twenty minutes to one.
I got it only last night at ten o'clock and I gave it back this morning to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I can only say that the earliest we could get it was about twenty minutes to one.

I might say to my hon. friend
that before it reached my office I had a telephone call that the file was wanted for the right hon. leader of the opposition. I retained it fifteen minutes, and it was then returned to the secretary.

I do not know
anything about the peregrinations of the file or how many people found it necessary to check it, but that is the hour it got to the office of the leader of the opposition.
I would like to point out to the hon. gentleman that the most of us do not know what he is talking about at all.

We will see if we can correct what perhaps is a common condition; we will see if we can make it a little less common. 1 am talking, Mr. Chairman, about the question of the export of power. My hon. friend forgets there was an arrangement under which this question was to be discussed under this item, and I am pointing out right
\

Supply-Trade and Commerce
at the commencement that I cannot give the House as well as I ought to give it, what is set forth under this file, and what the situation
is,	for I simply have not had the opportunity, I have not had the time to go into it.
I think we can say we are on common ground at the commencement. A lease was made-so far as I can make out in the short time I have had the chance of looking at this file-in June, 1911, which enabled, not this company but a predecessor of this company, to develop power at Carillon. There have been extensions to that lease from time to time; and it runs on until, in 1921, the lease is enlarged by a new document giving, as I gathered during the short time I have had the chance of looking at the lease, somewhat extended powers. I do not attempt to define them; the matter has run along from 1921 with extensions, so that it is still kept alive.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister and myself talked of this a little while on the last occasion when we were discussing this matter, and when I was attempting to find out whether any request had been made for the right to export power, whether anyone had been busy about it, whether anyone had seen him or any member of the government about
it.	Well, we might have saved a whole lot of time, for there is a very definite proposition before the government, as shown by the draft leases which are on this file. The proposition that is made to the government under these leases is that power shall be exported in the first instance to the United States, with the right to Canadian muncipalities to get of that power up to 100,000 horse-power. The main object of the undertaking is entirely the matter of the exportation of power to the United States, as I am going to show in a few minutes. I asked on the last occasion who was looking into this, who was pressing it, who was behind it, and my right hon. friend could not tell me anything; or if he could, he would not. I am going to give him now some information. There need be very little trouble now in finding out all about this matter.
The lease which is forwarded is forwarded under cover of a letter dated October 23, 1924. Two revised drafts are sent in. I point out that the file is incomplete at that point; I have seen nothing of former drafts; there is nothing of former correspondence. Whatever the peregrinations of the file were, it is quite clear that there is nothing to show on the file itself how this situation was led up to; but on the 23rd of October, 1924, we have a letter. I read a portion of it:

On behalf of the Carillon Industrial Corporation, Limited, I would like to submit for the consideration of the minister and the department, two revised drafts marked "A" and "B" respectively, and would be obliged if arrangements could be made to have these drafts reviewed with a view to a final agreement between the parties as to the precise form of the leases contemplated.
Yours sincerely,
Carillon Industrial Corporation Limited.
That communication is signed iby Miss Lyla Brennan, as secretary-treasurer. I cannot find in the telephone directory or anywhere else particulars as to the Carillon Industrial Corporation, Limited, but on inquiring as to Miss Brennan, I find from the directory that Miss Lyla Brennan is a stenographer in the office of McGiverin, Haydon & Ebbs, at 19 Elgin 'Street, Ottawa, and I might point out that this letter bears the address, 19 Elgin Street, Ottawa. So my right hon. friend has not far to go to get information as to who is behind this scheme and what is in it. All he has to do is to go to his senatorial friend, on the one hand, or to his member of the cabinet without portfolio, on the other hand, and he will have it.

speechtext: I do not know whether I fully grasped the purport of my hon. friend's remarks. Is he referring to my statement the other evening that the government had had no application before it? What my hon. friend is reading now as to some communications that have come to the minister and the department, I am hearing now for the first time. I had no knowledge of it at all until my hon. friend read the letter.
I am very, very sorry, Mr. Chairman, that in an important matter like this my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is being kept so much in the dark and does not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand
there are applications made departmentally running back three and four years. They have not come before the government; and I was speaking, as I said the other evening, for the government, and I made it quite plain the government had not considered any applications of the kind. I repeat that now.

My hon. friend
is doing scant justice to himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not at all.

and said I was not concerned with any formal application, but that I wanted to know whether

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend at the time was pressing for a statement from the government as to what they purposed doing in the export of power, and he spoke particularly of Carillon. I told him then that the government had not had that matter before them for consideration, and I repeat it.

My hon. friend
had better look at Hansard. What I was trying to find out was what was going on in connection with this matter, not what the government was going to do, but who was behind it.

Is that draft signed or is
it blank?

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman, who happens to be a lawyer, whether he ever heard of a draft document signed? If they were signed, they would not be drafts; they would be executed documents. We were trying to find out whether there was any real movement on, whether the deputations were accidental deputations; and we could get no information. But we have it here. We have an application for the export of power on a grander scale than anything we have ever had; that is the plain straight fact. And we also get it from the firm of McGiverin, Hay don & Ebbs, so there ought to be no mystery about it. Surely the government can find out and give the House and the country information as to who is behind this scheme. Well, I turn to the draft contracts and 'there are two. I confess in commencing that I have not had sufficient time to go through these contracts for the purpose of dissecting them and seeing clearly whether they differ one from the other. However, I have gone through them sufficiently to enable me to arrive at this conclusion-that the plain intent and the plain object under both contracts is the exportation of power in large volume and in large quantities. I first deal with contract A-
It is not a contract.

Well, draft contract A, submitted by the company to my
hon. friend. The covenant reads-I skip the first part of it which is not directly material:
Doth lease-
That is, the government.
unto and vest in the company the following rights, privileges and hydraulic powers on the terms and conditions and for the times in this indenture specified.
I' may say, just at this point, Mr. Chairman, that the contract runs a long time. In the first instance, if this lease is signed, it is to run to the 1st January, 1964. speechtext: Does my hon. friend think the government will entertain any such absurd request?

So, Mr. Chairman, while I admit it is ridiculous, I frankly hesitate to predict bounds to the government's powers of erring and of error. So I will have to leave that particular thing to my hon. friends right there.
How does it compare with the contract of the Bridge River Power Company?

If my hon. friend wants
to be fair he should deal with this as a contract which is submitted, and not as a contract which has been acted upon.

I have said that often, have I not? I am just talking about

I just stop to point out there that I do not know from this file the amount of power that is to be developed. Perhaps my hon. friend the minister knows what the proposition is?

I would rather reply to
my hon. friend when he gets through; I do not want to interrupt him.

But I am
looking for'the interruption.
Oh, oh.
There goes the general chorus. There goes a chorus which is a real chorus, which can always be counted on to fill in. But just look where we are.
Does my hon. friend want me to answer him now?
I want the information because it might cut out a whole lot of what I have got to say.

As a matter of fact I have never read those proposed leases, and have never considered them for a minute. I never saw them until Friday last, and I was not considering them at all. Those leases have never been brought before me and I do not know what is in them.
That is not the question I asked my hon. friend.
What was it?
I asked my hon. friend how much power was proposed to be developed?
I do not know what is in the leases.

This does not
say.
In the case of the National Hydraulic I think there was a proposed development of 400,000 horse power; but I do not know what is in those leases because I never read them.

If this is an
extension of the former idea, under this contract the right would be given to raise the dam to a height not exceeding 133 feet, and if the old plant would produce 400,000 horse power I would assume this would produce a bit more.

The National Hydraulic
asked to raise the level of the water to 133 feet.

the same thing. Well then, we have a proposition looking to the development of 400,000 horse power. Out of that amount 100,000 horse power would go to the Canadian user; but he is given that right in such a way that if the idea was to see that no Canadians used the power at all it is pretty well looked after, having regard1 to the district, having regard to the municipalities to be served, and the like, because there is a limitation as to the amount that can be held over, the clause reading:
The company shall supply such electrical energy to such Canadian consumers in blocks of not less than 10,000 horse power and at reasonable rates and on reasonable conditions such rates and conditions (other than those herein specified) in the event of disagreement between the parties to be determined by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada.

By whom and how
delivered?

That particular
is not given at all. I suppose the company will have to hand it over to the municipality, but that is not covered. Then it says:
In the event of the total of such requirements being less than 100,000 horse power the company shall be obliged to furnish the remainder of such 100,000 horse power or any portion thereof on notice from the minister that the same is required by Canadian consumers.
But if they do not go into it, in the first instance, the right to give that notice is only at the expiration of the five-year period, January 1, 1931 and January 1, 1936, and so on. It is perfectly obvious that the real intent of the whole of this draft is to look after export, and that the provision that is put in as to Canadian users is just another smoke screen. Then as to their right of export this document says:
Such surplus of electrical power at the said works of the company as may from time to time during the terms and renewals contemplated by this indenture be available for disposition after the company has fulfilled its obligations in respect to Canadian supplies as hereinbefore defined may be disposed of by the company to customers in the United States or elsewhere subject to compliance with the requirements of this contract, and the company in addition to all other rights and powers granted to, conferred upon or possessed by it is hereby vested with and may exercise all the rights of the lessor to export such surplus electric power but over the transmission facilities of the company and in so doing shall be the agent of the lessor acting for the use and service of the crown.
I just point out there, that if any action is ever taken on this request, there is no necessity to get any license at all. The contract is plainly drawn for the purpose of getting around the aot as to the export of electricity. That act does not apply to the crown; it does apply to ordinary companies exporting. But in this case the applicant, the mysterious clients of Messrs. McGiverin, Haydon & Ebbs, with a view of getting round the point, have struck upon the novel idea of putting themselves in the position of the crown, exporting as agents of the crown and in right of the crown. A more absurd proposition I think could hardly be conceived. The only trouble is that my hon. friend did not throw it out long ago. It would be better if he had read it and thrown it out, and we would have saved some time.
Another clause is put in for the purpose of saying that as to that export business the company is to be left to themselves, because that clause is put in on behalf of the company, and provides that these people who make the contract can export and the whole export is to be left to them.
The other contract was very very largely the same. I frankly do not think there is any good in either of them, or that anything can be said in favour of either of them. They both have these long terms to run, they both nave the absolute right to export; and if they did not get that, if the substitution was not enough, there is another clause put in under which, under the further assurances, the government has the power to give them all the licenses that are necessary.
There is another clause to which I wish to draw my hon. friend's serious attention. I do not know whether he will tell us frankly and fairly that this whole thing is gone, but I want to tell him. The proposition is just as he says, to develop 400,000 horse-power. From what little we have heard about it, it will not be possible to develop that horsepower there. And the company do not think they can, because they have another clause in the contract which gives them the right to supplement this power with power obtained wherever they can get it. The effect of this audacious proposition is this:	Suppose there
were only 200.000 horse-power at Carillon and the company could show there was a demand in the United States for the whole 400.000 horse-power, then, under this ridiculous proposition, they would have the right to go anywhere else, get that power and export it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, these are very long contracts, and it would take some time to go through them, but I do not think it should be necessary to do that. I think the House :s entitled to a frank statement to-day from the government. The last time we were discussing this matter the government knew nothing about it. The last time we were dealing with the question no applications had been made.
Not to the government.

I do not know
any way in which the applications can be made except through the minister who has the matter in charge. Now sometimes subterfuge can get almost too thin.

Allow me to straighten
out the matter, and let the hon. member keep cool. There was no suggestion made that there had never been any application to the Department of Railways and Canals. I think the answer given by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) was a correct answer.
How would an application be made 'except to the government, through its official channel?

When I get through-

Will my hon. friend not answer the question?
When I get through.

But before you get
through?
I cannot answer until I get through. As a matter of fact, none of the applications was ever taken to the government by the Minister of Railways, and the government, never considered one of them.

It is like the
difference between Tweedle-dum and Tweedle-dee.
Tweedle-dum in this case is willing to take all the responsibility for what he did not do.

My experience
is that all applications considered by the government, treating the government collectively when sitting in council, came through the report of the minister, and I do not know how they could come to them in any other way.
They never made a report.

I do not know
how anyone could make an application except in the first instance by sending it to the department, and the application here is made to the department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend expressed it accurately that time. He said the only way a matter came to the government was on the report of the minister. Now, the government has never had it before them, because there was no report by the minister.
I agree with my hon. friend in that statement but my hon. friend is wrong-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. Now I
think it would shorten matters if I would apologize humbly to my hon. friend, I never intended to be wrong; I never intended to convey any other meaning than what I am expressing now, namely, that the government had received no report through any minister on this matter and had not considered it at all. As to what applications there may be in the departments, I cannot speak for the government. I was speaking for the government as a whole, and I think I made that point clear. There may be in different departments a thousand applications of which I have no knowledge. But I have and should have a knowledge of matters that come before the government on the report of a minister.

We shall take it in that way; but what I was trying to find out was whether this was being pressed and who was pressing. It can be pressed only through a department. My right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) thought I was referring to the council. I was not. There is, however, an end of that. The minister may tell us whether something is going on about this, whether the thing is absolutely dead. It should never have lived at all. What is the situation?
It has not been bom yet.
We are delighted to hear that; but I should like to know whether Messrs. McGiverin, Haydon & Ebb3 have any object in putting life into these dead bones or not, and who is behind the thing.

I confess that I am considerably puzzled to get the meaning of all this sort of thing. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has got hold of a draft contract of some kind which the government denies knowing anything about. Am I correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.
It has never been considered.

The Prime Minister says,
" hear, hear." The hon. member had better get a straight answer.
Mr. FORKE. The ex-Minister of Finance should tell us where he got this contract, how it came into his hands.

We asked that these papers, which are ordinary governmental, departmental papers, should be tabled in the usual way, just as in any other case, and they were laid on the table yesterday afternoon. They perambulated around a bit; I managed to get hold of them at twenty minutes to one, and I was apologizing for not knowing the whole details of the case. The reason for that was simply because I had not had time to study them. There is no mystery about these papers at all; the mystery is as to who is behind them, what is going to be done with them, whether a thing that ought to be thrown out at once will be thrown out.

Apparently this application
may have been sent into the government and it may never have been considered. That is as far as I can understand the matter. I do not know whether the proper thing was to

Supply-Trade and Commerce
put these papers on the table unless they had had some notice or consideration by the government. Perhaps I am floundering a little, but again I confess my ignorance. I should like to get at the bottom of this matter.

May I be permitted, as far as I can in my humble capacity, to throw a little light on it? In the first place, these papers were in the Department of Railways and Canals, the hon. gentleman 4 p.m. is quite right in that. It is questionable whether papers that had never been considered were covered by the request of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and I read his remarks carefully- but so that there could be no question as to the Department of Railways and Canals bringing down everything it could find high and low, I brought down correspondence even from Sir Robert Perks on the Georgian bay canal, because it referred to this particular stretch of water. Allow me to give a little history. My hon. friend was somewhat astray, but not materially. The first lease was given in 1908 at the Carillon dam where the canal is-and that is why the matter comes under the Department of Railways and Canals-to the late Crawford Ross to develop 250 horsepower,

just a small development is given along nearly all the canals in the system. In 1911, that lease was transferred to a company which, I think, is called the National Hydro-Electric. The lease was enlarged a little, some new clauses being put in, but I think the total development under that would be only 500 horse-power. As a matter of fact, that lease has been honoured by that company, and at Carillon at the present time and for some years there has been a development of 250 horse-power. These two leases for this small development were, I am glad to say, signed by myself as Minister of Railways and Canals. The 250 horse-power lease was operated and is still in operation. In 1913, when the late Mr. Cochrane was Minister of Railways and Canals, a new application was made to him by the same company, if I remember correctly, to allow development which would mean an increase in the height of water to 115 feet. The development under that would have been a great deal larger; I think it would have been 100,000 horsepower. The arrangement was made, but while the then Minister of Railways and Canals, the late Mr. Cochrane, had the lease prepared, it was never executed. Some time later, I think it was in October-the date is immaterial-

National Hydro-Electric. I do not wish to be held too closely to the names of these companies; the name has changed several times, but to my mind it is always the same people with a new company.

I have very grave doubt if any clause put in a lease would override the statute of the Department of Trade and Commerce which provides for regulations as to the term of export. It is a mistake to say that the restricted term of one year is in the statute. The statute which has been in force for some eighteen years is quite broad. It allows the government by* order in council to regulate the period for which export can be permitted. In fact it gives the Governor in Council quite broad powers, extending even beyond this one particular point. But as a matter of fact the export of power is, under these regulations, confined to the term of one year, and I am very doubtful if any contract such as my hon. friend has read would be legal; certainly no person could borrow money on it unless it were in conformity with the statute. Now, as to the export of power itself. My hon. friend has asked me a question as to what the government proposes to do. This question is one of great import. No government in this country, either federal or provincial, has ever declared itself against the export of power in practice-they have in theory, but never in practice. At the present time I am not expressing an opinion on the export of power.
I want to face it squarely. It is such a big question that conceivably conditions might arise at times when the export of power would be essential. It has arisen with the Hydro-Electric of Ontario when they admit it to be highly essential to export power. I am not criticizing that action.

My hon. friend is not putting that quite clearly. The HydroElectric of Ontario do not for one minute deem it necessary to export power. Unfortunately they are in a position where they cannot help themselves, they have got to export power.
Why have they got to do so?

Apparently my hon. friend has not studied that contract any more than he has this file. Within the last few months
the Ontario Hydro-Electric has asked for the right to export 45,000 horse power per year off peak load. That is because they can make some money out of it, of course.

I do not think my hon. friend should say that that is the policy of the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission. The position in Ontario is simply this. For the moment-I hope it is only very temporary-industrial Ontario is in such shape that they have now got this surplus power, and the commission are given the right to export it temporarily. And it is the same thing with the other producers.

I am asking, is the government in favour of that policy?

I am stating the government's policy. I am pointing out that my hon. friend's supposed policy the other night is not practicable; is not followed by his own friends in any province; is not followed by any government. In the production of power business demands that under certain circumstances, such as those existing in connection wiith the Hydro-Electric projects, an export of power should be allowed.
Temporarily.

I will come to that. I
want to nail it down fast and tight that the policy of any government looking to the welfare of the Dominion of Canada and to the development of power in Canada should not be a prohibition of the export of power under all circumstances to the United States; for the result would be at one fell swoop to bring about increased rates on the part of the hydro-electric power projects in Ontario as well as on the part of other companies.

Let me go a little further. My hon. friend (Mr. Manion) suggests that the export should be temporary; I am coming to that. The legislation of the parliament of Canada has been sane along these lines. The regulations adopted in 1907-08 by the Laurier administration were sane. They restricted by regulation under the statute the period of time for which licenses might be granted, limiting it at twelve months. That was wise. The hon. gentleman may say that that might permit the establishing of vested rights. What vested right could' be established in twelve months? None, and none has been so established. This regulation restricting the export of power to a period of twelve months is notice to the United States users that this supply of power to them is not permanent; that it can be taken away from them at the end of any twelve-months period. It is notice to every person concerned that this is only temporary. I want to put it again, as strongly as I can, that the policy of this government in, power is the policy that has been adopted in Canada and successfully followed during the last eighteen years. It is the policy that has been practised by the HydroElectric Commission of Ontario and1 by the companies, and it is a policy under which every interest is safeguarded so far as the Canadian user is concerned.

There are two or three

It is strange that we should have such vague terms as those to which the Minister of Railways has just given expression. policy. So far as I have ever heard there is no criticism of the granting of the right to develop. Everybody knows it has 'been before the government of Canada for months in a most prominent form. It has been the subject of importunities of delegations. It has been the subject of newspaper discussion. It has been the subject of acute controversy. It has been the subject of propaganda of a most skilful and pronounced type. In this state of affairs the government was asked on Thursday last where it stood on the matter, and specifically was asked whether an application had not been made to the government for the export of a large quantity of power from a proposed Carillon development. This same publication called the attention of the interested parties in the Ottawa valley district to the matter, and a big meeting was called in the town of Lachute, in the county of Argenteuil, where a resolution was passed protesting against the opposition, and endeavouring to show the government the benefit it would be not only to that particular district, but to the province and the Dominion as a whole, if the Carillon power development was approved. The question was viewed not only from the point of view of their own interest, but from the national point of view. The resolution read as follows:
Resolved that after consideration of the proposed hydro-electric development at Carillon, on the Ottawa river, the council and citizens of the town of Lachute express their approval of the project and request that the federal and provincial governments do give their immediate endorsement to the work so that the work of construction may proceed without delay.
In endorsing the project, this meeting wishes to point out .that the construction of this large hydroelectric plant would ensure an abundant supply of electrical energy, now so urgently needed throughout the Ottawa valley; that it would mean the expenditure of many millions of new capital in this province; that it would give employment to thousands of workmen, thus relieving the serious situation now facing civic and other authorities; and that it would create activity in many industries manufacturing materials needed for such an undertaking.
A further consideration which this meeting considers is highly important to Lachute is that the development at Carillon would be accompanied by the construction of a 14-foot canal from St. Anne's to Ottawa, thus creating a new navigable waterway which would assist in industrial development, without the cost of a single dollar to the public.
Resolved further that as it is reported that this huge power development is not financially possible unless there is an immediate market for the surplus power, this meeting can see no reason why the export of power should not be permitted so long as the home demands are amply met-a provision which can be fully provided for by the federal government.
That resolution, Mr. Chairman, covers all the points in favour of the granting of the electric water-power plant at Carillon. Firs of all, it would mean the expenditure of mans millions. The plant, as shown by the en gineer's estimate, would cost about $52,000,000, with a capacity of 400,000 horse-power. The erection of that plant would mean employment for over 2,000 people during three years, and the employment of that number of people for that length of time would certainly bring relief to the general labour situation in Canada.
Not only do t'he municipal councils in the districts north and south of the Ottawa river support the proposition, but the Trades and Labour Council of the city of Montreal adopted a resolution in its favour similar to the one passed at Lachute. It is therefore apparent that labour men to the number of
100,000	are behind the people of the Ottawa valley in the support of the enterprise. The Trades and Labour Council of Montreal, adopted also a resolution approving the project.
In addition to the great good to labour that will result from the carrying out of the enterprise, there is the further fact that navigation will be facilitated by the raising of the level of the Ottawa river. From the engineering reports that are available it is evident that the carrying out of the project would give a fourteen foot waterway in the Ottawa river, thus placing the city of Ottawa, on a footing

No capitalist will invest money in an enterprise unless there is a guarantee of at least twenty-five years' tenure, and that is what the National Hydro Electric is asking for. Then too, unless a market is found for the surplus power outside of Canada the process of developing electric energy will be slow and tedious, and Canada itself will lose money which would1 otherwise come to it as a result of the development and sale of power.
As regards the development of our power resources, not only in this province, but throughout Canada, I maintain that without finding a market for our surplus power outside the Dominion our development of electrical energy will be slow and tedious and we will still go on losing millions of dollars a year which would come to Canada as a result of the sale of power. I am convinced that the opposition which is apparently emanating from interested sources, if allowed to succeed, will mean the absolute killing of the Carillon power development which is so vital to the people of the Ottawa valley, and unless those opposing the export can give us more concrete arguments that the sale of electrical energy should not be permitted, I am certain that the federal authorities will understand the workings of the "power ring," which is slowly but surely getting a strangle hold on the power situation throughout our province.
What is the objection which is urged to this project? It is that "we may need in the future the surplus power proposed to be exported." Surely this is not a reason for deferring action in connection with this very important matter.

I have been very much interested by the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Ethier), but he does not quite prove his case. He rather proves the argument that I am going to make in favour of delay in this matter. My suggestion in a word is this, and I have written it down rather carefully. The thing for the government and parliament to do in regard to the export of power is to delay further action until federal investigation is made, first, as to our possible water-power development, and second, as to its further conservation by the use of long-distance transmission by high tension current, as scientists now promise us. Such an investigation might result in a national policy of keeping this power as a national asset which, in time, would take care of our public debt and our national budget for many, many years. Such a policy would have to be strengthened by a programme of sustained rainfall, by forest preservation, and permits to export power should be, not for long periods, but for short periods with frequent renewals. What the power people are trying to get-and I direct the attention of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to this-is to sew up the country in long terms for the export of power. Even with the frequent renewals as I propose, the result may be that this, which I consider is the greatest asset that Canada has to-day, namely, the possibility of the development of our waterpower, will pass from the people into the hands of entrenched monopoly. Therefore,

there is every reason why we should conserve this power. We should see whether it is not possible, as scientists say, to transport it for long distances by high tension currents. Besides that, they say now that electrical energy can be transmitted by a beam. Just what a beam is I will not undertake to say at the . moment, but they have that in their mind. They say something else about water-power. A water-power is the most marvellous thing in the world. Neither a gold deposit nor a silver deposit is to be compared with it, nor even are the great wheat fields. This hydroelectric power, once you generate it, has this peculiar characteristic. Once you store the water and put in your generator, you get the power and what does the power do? It delivers itself a hundred miles, and I hope, in a little time, a thousand miles away through a wire; it requires no upkeep and it becomes more and more valuable. The scientists are promising a still further development and that is this. All hon. members know what these little storage batteries are. They see them in the hardware stores. The scientists promise even to store water-power in the same way and they say that it can be kept for years; that it can be transported and then released at any distance away where it can be distributed by other wires. Parliament, therefore, ought to take care of this asset. It should not part with it; especially it should not part with it under long-term 9 p.m. leases, but it should keep it as the greatest asset the country has. To prove that it is the biggest asset the country has, one needs only to listen to the testimony that my hon. friend has just given to the committee about the efforts of capitalists in this country and throughout the whole of the United States to get this great source of electrical power sewed up to their companies, because if they get that, they have an almost unlimited field of profitable distribution of it. Canada has this wonderful store. Notwithstanding the statement that has been made, I contend that we ought not to lease any of this power for export until we know whether there will be enough of it for ourselves; and, above all, we ought to keep the development in our hands until there has been a thorough investigation as to its amount.

I hold to this policy, and I dare say it is one that may not find support in some quarters of the House. I hold that the great water-powers of Canada are among the most valuable resources that this country retains. Now from the very nature of it, electrical energy on the rivers of Canada can only be developed by a large investment of capital, and I hold absolutely to this principle, that that development should be under public aegis, and should not be done by private capital. I do so for this reason: I recall, if I may give an experience of which I have knowledge, that in the province of Manitoba we had a private power development, the first that was undertaken and carried through in that province. In 1906 the citizens of the city of Winnipeg were paying 16 cents per kilowatt hour for power to light their homes, and were paying about the same rate for power to drive their machinery. The city of Winnipeg thought that rate was too high and it approached the private power company with a view to securing an arrangement for a lower rate. It was unable to make an arrangement with the power company, although it offered them a very advantageous bargain. I think as a matter of fact the power company held out for some ten or twelve cents per kilowatt hour, while the city wanted to negotiate on a basis of eight or nine cents. Failing to reach an agreement, the city of Winnipeg at that time undertook its own power development on the Winnipeg river, and brought that power into the city over a distance of eighty miles, and the day the transformer started to work the rate was three and one-third cents per kilowatt hour, with a ten per cent discount for cash, and it has remained at that point ever since. Not only have the citizens of Winnipeg had in consequence the great advantage of cheaper light and power, but the city by careful

management has built up very handsome reserves, and within the last year the revenue from the power made a contribution of $100,000 towards relieving the city taxation. That is an outstanding example, but one that can be duplicated anywhere in this country, and I say that this vast resource, the value of which is only beginning to be realized, should not be turned into private hands for private exploitation. I would have the water-powers in the valley of the St. Lawrence from the headwaters of the Great Lakes to the Atlantic ocean developed by public money. I would not have them distributed and sold by public money, but I would have them made available to every manufacturer and to every city in Canada that wanted to use that power, and I would give it to those manufacturers and to those cities at cost. In that way you would place our manufacturers and cur artisans in a much more favourable position to compete with the whole world.

I agree altogether with the argument of my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Baldwin), who stated that within a comparatively few years-I think he put it at some twenty-five or thirty years, and that is a comparatively short period in the history of a country-all this power would be required in Canada. I agree with him. I look forward to the time when this country will have not the eight or nine or ten millions that it has now, but fifty or sixty or seventy-five or even one hundred millions of people, and that will come within the present century, or almost so, I believe. When that time comes, shall we not require all this power, and more, in Canada? And what position are these central provinces of Ontario and Quebec in with respect to the development of power? What other agency is there for the development of power in these provinces outside of the water in your lakes and streams? You can bring in coal from a foreign country, it is true, but you may have that shut off some day, and while you have coal down in the extreme east of Canada the cost of bringing that coal to develop electrical' energy, for instance, in the heart of Ontario is very considerable, and I have never had any very great hope that the needs of Ontario and Quebec in the matter of fuel, and particularly Ontario, can be met by the coal mines of Alberta or the mines at Sydney, for the distance is too great. Mr. Chairman, I brought this question to the attention of the minister last Friday. Unfortunately I was out of the House to-day attending the aimless Ocean Rates committee and therefore have missed most of the discussion. But since last Friday I have carefully looked up the act under which the government is authorized to export this power, and also the regulations. I want to present to the government a viewpoint prompted by the remarks of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). The legislation which empowers the government to act in regard to the export of power was passed in 1907. I think every hon. member will admit that the development of electrical energy in 1907 and

Supply-Trade and Commerce
its general commercial use was in such a condition of partial experiment-I was going to say, infancy-that it is not a safe guide for our actions to-day. In other words, the problem of to-day is the outgrowth of a number of years; it is one of those things that develops gradually, perhaps unnoticed, until we get to a point where there is some sudden and large development in view, and then we come to a realization of the direction in which we are heading. That condition is before us now. Here ds a huge proposition facing Canada-I am going to refer to it in a little more detail in a moment-and Canada, not only the government, is now determining what its course and its policy will be in a few years. I therefore suggest to the government that this whole busines with respect to further licenses for the export of power should be held in abeyance until the act under which we are at present working can be carefully surveyed and studied by parliament. I do not think it can be done this year, but the government should make a survey of the matter during the recess and next session we might revamp the whole act and bring it up to date. Let me review the act' very briefly. It is very brief and general in its terms. It is 6 and 7 Edward VII, chapter 16, assented to on April 27, 1907. It has some very simple provisions. .First, no person shall export power without a license. No person shall construct a power line for export without a license. The Governor in Council-this is an important provision-may grant licenses upon such conditions as he thinks fit, and such licenses shall be revocable upon such notice as the Governor in Council may deem reasonable. In other words, the whole thing is placed in the hands of the government and the Governor in Council. Then it provides that such licenses may be limited as to quantity; it does not say "shall" be limited. The government is empowered to-day under this act to grant a 120 year lease-issue a 120 year license-or a 99 year, or a 40 or a 20 year license. I cite 120 for a certain reason which probably is better understood by the government than by most members. Then, the Governor in Council may make regulations not inconsistent with 'the act, and so on. Now, there are certain regulations that are also not up to date; they were adopted the same year that the act was passed, as the date upon those I have in my hand indicates. I want to refer briefly to the regulations. One clause refers to the quantity proposed to be exported; it must be shown in the license. There is another clause, an important one, which provides that the license shall be revocable at the will 
of the Governor in Council if the licensee refuses or neglects to comply with any of the conditions from time to time imposed by the Governor in Council. At once you see that the revocability, to use the term of the license, depends on whether or not the licensee violates the conditions that are imposed upon him. In other words, if he observes the conditions his license is not a revocable license, so far as that particular provision is concerned. Then it says that if the electrical energy, gas or fluid is required for the use of Canadian producers in Canada, any such license shall be revocable upon such notice to the licensee by the Governor in Council as the Governor in Council deems reasonable in such cases. What does that mean? If there seems to be a need of power in Canada, then it is the wish or the will or the whim of the Governor in Council which must determine whether or not the license shall be cancelled. Under this regulation the matter is entirely in the hands of the government.

Of course governments have to carry on between sessions of parliament, and there is no other power to cancel but the Governor in Council. It is possible that action could not await the meeting of parliament.

Quite true. I am not saying this is wholly wrong; I am simply pointing out the facts. Both the regulations and the act are of a character that require careful revision. The other clause I desire to refer to is this:
Where a supply of electrical energy is provided in any part of Canada by the contractor for export and home consumption, then the price charged to any person or company in Canada by the contractor shall not exceed the price at which the electrical energy is sold by the contractor for export in like quantities under similar circumstances.
Now, I understand a contract was entered into by one of the power companies many years ago under which power is being exported to the United States at $12 per horsepower-I am subject to correction, but I think I am stating it correctly-whereas the same company is selling power in Canada at double or treble that amount. They could not sell in Canada at the figure to-day; it is an old contract. The Governor in Council is empowered to say to that company: You must sell your power in Canada at the same rate as you do for export. The government will not suggest for a minute that they could or would make any such suggestion to the Hydro-for I think it is a subsidiary of the Hydro which is affected in the case to which I refer. That clause in the regulations, there-

fore is of no value where the contract price is below what is a reasonable figure for the sale of the power.

There is a distinction to be made between companies who entered into contracts before this law was passed and those who did so subsequently. The former were not supposed to presume that such a law would be passed, although of course theoretically they are subject to it if the government wished to make it applicable to them. But is it reasonable to suppose that any company that entered into a contract after the law was passed in 1907 would know that they would be subject to the terms of that statute at any time that the Governor in Council thought it necessary to enforce the regulation providing for a limit of one year.

That is quite true. I am mentioning this not by way of complaint or criticism of the government, but rather to lay before the committee the difficulties which undoubtedly have developed and to offer a warning against a continuance or increase of those difficulties. I want to say a very few words in regard to the present situation. I admit frankly that necessarily my information is not very definite, but I think it comes from a sufficiently high source to justify my offering it to the committee. There is in existence to-day, I am told, a very large and powerful syndicate of American and Canadian capitalists who are desirous of developing a considerable amount of electrical energy and a large number of hydro-electric powers in eastern Canada for the purpose of supplying power to the United States and eastern Canada. The idea is to develop it on lines that will ensure to certain sections of the United States an ample supply of power. Involved in this is the American interest in the international waterway so I am told. Now then we ought to be very careful how we proceed. I am also informed that the first unit they desire to develop is the Carillon power; that is to be the first in a number of units of power development. They are asking -this is in their programme, so my information goes-for 400,000 horse-power from the Carillon development, whereas it is well known, so I am also informed by competent engineers, that the maximum to be developed from the Carillon power will be 200,000 horsepower. If that is the case, they are seeking to tie the country to an export of 400,000 horse-power, the balance of which will have to come out of some other power plant in some other section. This, I believe, is fairly near to the mark. If it is near to the mark,
then I say it behooves the government of Canada to pause before they become a party to it. The issuing of a permit or the entering into of an agreement which will obligate this country to the export of power for any given period of years to my mind is a very, very serious menace to the industrial future of this country, a most serious menace, and I really do not believe that the government or parliament or the people of Canada appreciate how serious it is. I do not think we can understand it until we have given it a great deal more study than we have at the present time. It is beginning to filter into our minds through the reports that are made by engineers. I admit that many of these reports are conflicting, but some of them are alarming, and some of them are exceeding significant in the evidence and the data they produce. Therefore I again put it to the government that I think it would be a fair statement for them to make to parliament that nothing will be done for one year, or until parliament meets again, until the whole question of power development and power exportation can be fully studied and the legislation which is now on the statute books be revised and brought up to a point where it will properly and adequately safeguard Canada's interests. I do ask the government to-night to stay its hand in regard to any agreement, and in regard to the issuing of any license or the entering into of any understanding with any company that will commit this country ,to participation in this great scheme which I have not the slightest doubt from the information I have [DOT] is already well under way and in a stage of fairly advanced development.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say the government have already taken that position.

I am very glad to hear the Prime Minister say that. Do I understand that the government's position is that they will do nothing for a period of one year until parliament has had an opportunity of studying this problem, which I think is the proper course to pursue?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government has stayed its hand for many months in this matter, and it does not intend to proceed with any haste whatever.

I want to say to the
Prime Minister-and I am not captious at all, I welcome his observation-but I would welcome much more the assurance that nothing will be done along the line I have indicated, that is in committing this country to anything more than the bare annual license.

I add to that, Mr. Chairman, and I put this to the Prime Minister, it is what I stated the other evening, and what I have already repeated to-night, that within the period of the last twenty-five years, and the last twenty years in particular, there has grown up a condition which was not foreseen when this act was passed in 1907, under which the government permits licenses to be issued for the export of power. Therefore I say to the Prime Minister further than what I have already stated, I believe the time has come, and we are warned by present events, when we should refrain from issuing even any further licenses for export, and in saying that I am not condemning the government for the licenses that have been issued or criticizing the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier or the Conservative government that followed in any sense; I am not criticizing any government, but I say that conditions are such that we are warranted as a parliament, and the government is the executive of parliament, in staying our hand absolutely from issuing any further export licenses.

that since the government has been in office, at no time has a license been issued beyond a period of one year. That is the policy upon which the goverment has been proceeding, and that is the policy upon which it intends to proceed.
